A telegram, dated la bore, Friday, nays: To-day the Calml emennission condemned ...teeth 10 prisoners. including one of the mailmen, of the vellum,. The total killed in the recent lighting arts 90, including 20 officers, the wounded 290. The bodies of Captain Opens, of the 720 d, and Captain Ilardy, of the artillery, and Lieutenant Forbes, of the 14th Bengal Cavell-1, have been recovered. Fetalen news leas been received of the lighting since the defeat of the the enemy, on the 23n1. The telegraph wires are entirely destroyed as far as Jundelluck. Since the complete defeat of the enemy's attack upon the canton- ments upon the Zird, we have been occupied in scalering the last remain, of Ike Afghan forces. As far as power of Resistance went their army ceased to exist at the moment when the cavalry brigade charged down upon them :es taey returrml from their attack upon the corner of the Berm no Hill, where the infantry and guns drove off the enemy to the east. Thus in • moment the greatest nombinition ..1 native tribes Afghanistan hall known for a century fell all to pieces. The native accounts sav that in all 61,000 men answered to Maltomet Jan's appeal. Our one calculations, however, never 'Mice the numbet which have appeared around Cabul :et more than 40,000. The natives exert that the Kohistan contingenta were fully 20,000 strong. It i. with pletsure that we draw attention to an announce- ment in our advertising columns thst, under the ausuims of the Over and Wharton Liberal Association, a public meeting will be held in the Winsford Town Hall, on Thursday evening next. It is gratifying to find that the Liberals in Cheshire are not content with merely forming district election committees and an executive council, but are bent upon employing all legitimate means for ousting front the reprewntation of the divisiun the two gentlemen who have hitherto given their un- divided support to the reckless and extravagant policy of . the Beaconsfield administration. That recklessness and ex- travagance, we doubt not, will be fully and clearly exempli- fied by the gentletnen who are ath ertised to deliver addresses on the occasion. Mr. George P Wilbraham, of Delamere Home, will preside over the meeting, and among ' the speakers will be Mr. G. W. Latham, of Bradwall Hall; Dlr. Begot Molesworth, the second Liberal candidate for Blackburn; Mr. Jo hinter, of Woodford Hall, and other gentlemen. It in tolilroped that the Liberals of Wimford will muster in strong force, and show by their earnestness their dislike of. policy of bluster and fireworks that is pro- of commercial distrust and aufferingand of increased national taxation.

EXTRAORDINARY tinow-ru IN Toe RseastaLts Verve Or Wtones.—At the Widnes Seseions, on Wednesday, a new poor-rate of 2. in the £ was signed by the sitting magistrates. It will doubtless interest our readers to know that since the last asseasment, in 1875, the increase in the gross rateable value has been £27.000. The present rate is calculated to raise £9,000 The overseers laid the last rate no the 2.301 February last, and it has thus run a little over ten Inont IN. We understand that the calls upon them have amounted to £3,000 more thin the noon for which they had calculated ; and the rate now laid is to raise money the pay- ment of which has been demanded within ten days, or the overseers mono lee sued. The late was laid in 1877, and it is stated that the present difficulty is consequent upon that state of LICILSI and the generally depress,' state of trade. div.p: THE GREAT It OF LEAD IN WIDNES.

At the Widnes Police Court, yesterday, James Ince, James Trainor, William McNally, Patrick McPartland, and Miotnoel McPartland were brought up on remand charged with stealing 3 cwt. 1 qr. 14 lbs. of old and new lead, value ,£2 18s, the property of Messrs. Hall and Shaw, chemical manufacturers, some time between the Iltb and 3lsl Decent- , bee—Mr. Dwyer, coal dealer, was charged with stealing and receiving the lead, knowing it to have been stelen.—Mr. I Husband appeared for the prisouers Ince and Trainor, and Mr Beasley represented the other prisoners.—At the begin- I fling of the case the prisoner Dwyer seemed much affected with the position in which he was placed, and wept very much.

Peter Tolman, foreman plumber for Molars. Hall and Shaw, said he lived in White-street, Runcorn. Owing to what was said to him on the Ist instant, lie examined on derneath the chatnbers at his employers' works, and missed the sheet of lead, weighing about 3i cwt., which he was able to don- City. The lead had not been mid to anyone by the firm. 'The weight of the lead was 3, cwt. lqr. 14 lbs., and it was worth about £2 18s.
er;as-examination by M. Beaaley, witnew, ellid that when he wae employed a Messrs. Pilkington's, the prisoner Dwyer worked under him as a plumber's labourer. . .

Wm. Melton, plumber, John-street, employed by the prosecutora, identified a piece of lead eight feet ire length. fle had worked 114 MTlellantra, Muspratt's and Golding Davis's, but at nory of thene places did they employ tar in potting in gutters..

r-J0h174 ilca7an, a boy, said he had lived witlf Dwyer from the 20th December. He remembered New Year's Day, when the prisoner McNally came into the stable at the place, Dwyer being there at the time. McNally asked for I,wyere but he (Dwyer) said it was not well, but he could have another which was in the stable. McNally agreed to take the one offered, and he and Dwyer'went not and yoked the pony. The two returned in about two hours with the pony and cart. The persons with the pony mut cart were James Trainor, James Ince, Patrick McPartland, and Wm. McNally. They all assisted in pulling and pushing the cart lnto the yard limn the greet. Ile noticed some lead at the bottom of the cart, part of it being in sacks and the rest loose. When the cart hod been taken into the yard the four men began to carry the lead from it into the stable; and whilst they were so engaged two policemen entered the place. He (witness) was holding a lighted candle at the time, and there was another lad, coned Kenny, with him. Thomas Kenny, aged 14, who is employed by Dwyer, in selling coal, gave evidence in support of the evidence of the Loot witness.

P.C. Clarkson stated that on the night of the 3lst ult, he on ant, 0 Waterleo-road, and saw the prisoner Dwyer in charge of a pony and cart. P.C. Pitt on the night of the 3lst December went with P.S. Vickers to the premises of the prisoner Dwyer, in William-street.Mill-hrow. On entering his yanl he saw a pony and cart, conWning sacks full of lead. Trainor wee sitting on one of the sacks in the cart, and wten he saw him (witness) coming towards him he got down. He took Trainor into the stable, where he cow McNally taking a piece of lead ! out of Patrick McPartland'a hand. The prisoner Ince was ' close by at the time. He aka nix or seven pieces of lead in ne of the stalls. On entering the stable he said to the pri- soners, "Stand back, all of you." The other prisoners said they had brought the lend there without D‘eyer's knowledge. He enunired where they got they got the lead from, but they made no answer. He sent for assistance, and upon other officers arriving upon the scene he took all the prisoners and the lead to the station. In answer to the charges, Dwyer said " I know nothing about it." Sergeant Vickers corroborated, and proved taking the prisoners into custody. Mr. Beasley (to witness): I suppose that your only reason for apprehending the prisoner Michael McPartland was he- lie was in the neighbourhoml of the stable. The case, as force he is concerned, has not gone beyond suspicion, I suppose? NVitnes", I think not. . _

Lamb against Thomas Holden, for an alleged trespass com- mitted by time on premises in the occupation of the plain. tiff.—The plaintiff is tenant of • house in Jackson's-lane, Heath-road, Runcorn, owned by James Catterall. On either , side of the house is a dwelling, owned by the defendant. ! I The alleged trespass was the removal of a 'Spout, and the I :substitution of a line of spouting (mu, the defendant's pro-1 I perty, which. it wasolleged, hod the effect of throwing the ' water on totter plaintiff's property, instead of it going into the course through which it has flowed for the last 24 years. Since the houses were built, the line et spouting has run under the eaves, the whole length of the three houses, but in Julv last the defendant cut the spouting near to where the plaintiff's house connects with onset the defendant's, and mode a spout upon Limb's house. A tub wan placed at the bottom of the spout to receive the water. It was alleged Shot the tub had overdowed very much and in September last, the water, first communicating with a cesspool close to the building, entered through the foundation, and so made the dwelling unfit for human habitation. On the scrimmage being formed the Brackley forwards dribbled ' the ball into Warrington quarter, Edwards relieving with a long "pont.' div.head: MEETING OF WIDNES LIBERALS.
div.p: MEETING OF WIDNES LIBERALS.
FATAL ACCIDENT AT WIDNES. ONE MAN KILLED AND ANOTHER SERIOUSLY

I Yestenlay morning an accident happened at the works of Messrs. James Mu pearl and Ca.. chemical manufacturers, Anne-street, East, Widnes, by which one was killed and another so seriously injured that he is not expected to re- cover. It appears that at about eleven o'clock a number of men, including the two above-nienti.,ned, wereengaged in putting together the parts of an acid trough, which is made of four inimense flags. The stones were hoisted into the required position by rne.lns of a block and chain—what is known as a tripod being used for the purpose—and whilst the men were busily engaged, one of the llags,,,f the enormous weight of two tons, fell upon two of them, the one being canted John Riley, aged 24, of Manchester, and the other Patrick Kelly, about 311 years of age, of Pitt-street, Widnes. Riley:who had only come from Manchester on the previous night, and started working at the manufactory that loom- ing, was killed instantly, and Kelly was no saiously hurt that but very little hope was entertained of Ids recovery , when enquiries were uncle by our representative last tight. The unfortunate man wasaltended by Dr. O'Keeffe, and by his directions removed to the Widnes Cottage Hospital in a cab. Riley's body was taken to the Hospital dead-house. We understand that the accident arose owing to the flag not haying been properly 'stayed." Information has been for- warded to the coroner, and An inquest will probably be held on Monday when all the circrunstances of the case will doubtless he thoroughly investigated.

Sir,—l have observed from an article or letter in the Nor! lorich Guardian that the Conservatives of Northwich are taking the alarm because hi, in cootemplation to raise, renew or replace with soma more convenient structure the bridge over the river Weaver. Now, to thy mind, which I do not often declare in print, it would bet very greet im- provement to the tragic which keeps the population of the district with bread ilighe bridge were raieed or a pontoon drawbingo sulrt Ruff& 'the river I'd eaveris the great trade highway of the county, and though the inhabitants of the town of Nort hatch alight, as no doubt the old Conservatives j would, as usual, complain of any improvement instinctively, yet I claim for the great trade highway a Met consideration, ant asecondary one only fur the town of Northwich,orrather ita few gnininlves. SIR COLBERT OREENALL'S GREAT SPEECH, [NUMBERS XXII, 28 v. 3 Ste,—ht last the long silence is broken. Long awl alxiously have we recited, and DOW our patience is rewarded. low rialy rewarded only those can tell who know. Sir Gill;ert the Silent, the last, if the least, et the Tory expositors of the creed of Benjamin, has been giving tre en authoritative explanation of the cause of the bad trade and commereid depression which weigh no heavily mane us. With that native modesty which sits ea well upon Ida,. charaettristic of true and intrinsic greatnesa be chose oath° scene of hi, aLstesinanlike utterances the her parlour of a village public rather than our Public Hall; and for an audience certain local farmers, his tenants and dependants, .other than the larger and posailly more CT itical hearers to be found in the town which by courtesy lie is said to repre- sent. Whatever monetary qudilications may he requir. d for an M.P. it is very evlent from the :mom. of fechic tnaddle which found 500 Von's Day ;,i010" n Arms" twhatevor they uLty be— posdbly a beet barrel rampod sup- ported by drunkards reconthent—dropm,l, to represent the tears of widow, arid orphans) that the intelle,total require- ments are very indeed. and need deter no man, how- ever great a duller he may he, from seekina, and if he ha well gilt, obtaining this timeh-curetedsnd oft ntisplaced doe- It appears that, according to the prophet Gilbert, ° Eng- land will prosper whilst the Queen lives." This is not say- ing much br her successor! Perhaps in his next utteranco Sir Gilbert vrill enlighten ore. to the mune of this, and what connection there is between the two things? Ako why we, who have been living this last year or no beneath her bene- ficent ruleand had the ineetitnable blessing oft Tory Govern- ment, should, despite these advantages, have been brought so near national bankruptcy e The puerility of the associa- ties, approaches the sublnne—the sublimity of absurdity. It required aOOO great—in at least one sense—to give it birth. .•.. .• . •.

"*.Salting aside all personalities and regarding it as a matter of pi Mein!, there ore a great many people who think that royalty in England is a very fancy article fot which, an for all fancy articles, we hews to pay a very fancy price. They think, Mr. Editor, and I don't altogether olisagtee witti then, that it is merely an article of luxury and ore,oeb ought to be pairt for by those who enjoy it. I don't. Royalty in England is a farce, and not a laugh Ode but a very expen- sive one. The portent generation had no voice in the dis- posal of the immense autos anoudly thrown away in this gunner, they Iwing then too young to be consulted in the matter, but I live in hopes that when the guention comes to be reopened they will demand a change and o great reduction. if not no entire abolition, of this yearly waste of the public money. But if all this happen.. what on earth will become of the manufacture of baronets? ith the Sovereign would die , the means of rewarding with titles and distinctions meaM I originally an the reward of bravery or wow conspicuous not : of heroism, those bumble political followers who, with sufli... cient subser% iency, had done the dirty work of the party. ; This great speech is also very ouggestive—more in whnt i it does not sty than in the thought. we find there. Not a i word ahout the misery which the speaker had helped hie ; maelers tin more senses thm one) toscatterbroadcaat through the world the unnecessary wars and tt.e nee.ssary poverty and taxation which must follow. The first thing they wanted was to do right," says Sir Unhurt Grernall. But what is right? felt "right" to raise this nation try warlike speeches to a frenzy of Jingoism, and then to hound it Onto attack with fire and sword another and a friendly one? Is it right by to doing to increase poverty at home and to add greatly to burdens of the poor people of India? We in England, who have hart tome voice in the election of the perpetrators of these wicked- news, may grin and abide the punishment, as the well- deserved penalty for our electoral nine, whether of commis- eine or omission : but the case is very different with the 1 poor ryot of India. He—a slave in all but name—already on the verge of starvation, will be farther ground down, and made to pay, through the medium of the abominable Salt Tax, which might very properly be called 0100 upon health, so erwential in this article to residents in countries no far 1 from the non. I' hrough this odious impost, he will be called npon to contribute his share of the expense of this nnneces- sary Afghan war. To him this war will be an unmitigated I evil, brought about not only without hie consent,but agitinst his will, and for what? Simply that we may robin quiet poseessionf Ms country ! In order to thwart our supposi- tions enemies, we compell hin to furnish Ore (unto. Is this right? In my humble opinion it is alavery, with the added inoult of calling it freedorn.—l am, nit, soriowfully your', JOHN PEERS. 66, Buttirmarket-street, IVarrington.

The MAYOR moved that the minutes of the Watch Conn mittee be confirmed. Councillor Ilaunisowsecomled the motion. Alderman Ttanwtts inquired 'shadier any steps wend being taken with regard Coo atesto fire engine? Ile did think ' it wan highly imported that this borough ought to have al steam fire engine. Ile had nothing whatever to do with :he expenae, but it was really an essentiaiity, as their engines were not aufficiently aatisfactory. Supposing they Ikad a fire at Cockhedge factory, or Mr. Fairclough's care mill, or any other high elevation, they had not sufficient power Co work by manual Palau, That subject had keen brought before the Council repeatedly, but he did not nee any pro- gress being made. Ile wanted to tee emne headway made with regard to the introduction eta steam fire engine into Warrington. Councillor Kean, said the comtnitlee were losing no time whatever. They were simply preparing a house to receive the steam fire engine, and as soon as the houge was ready they ' would tum their attention lair. It would be a pity t'o has 4 a Mee., fire engine and no place to put loin. It they would Mke a walk on Co Heath limb they would see that the new fire engine station Wan progressing favourably. Councillor Sorrow said the question was often considered by the old fire engine committee, and one of the obstacles that was considered in the way at the time, beeidee the re- quirement of a buiPing for a steam fire engine, was the queslloll an to the for 'not water in the town. "--Ald;;Men Tunartas : Under all circumstances let or hdve a Meant fire engine. Alderman Hoaxes did not believe there wee eft aligbte.d necesaity lore gleam fire engine. _ Thr monthly imwting of the Runcorn Improvement Corm unasioners was held on Monday. Mr. Lyon preended, and there were also pretwnt Messrs. Norman, Williams, P. Speakm in. McDougall. Meadowcrolt, Shaw, Briscoe, Marshall. ',Maker Law Clerk), Mouritz Medical Officer). BrookeMSecretary), and. Barker (Surveyor).

. . TRARIA •MD MONTHLY MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT. The report of Mr. SIDERITE. medical officer, was an follows There wore 29 deaths registered in Runcorn during the month of December. 1879. in,ing an annual mortality of about 21 per 1000. Of thew f,ve were due to cerebral affections, five to phthisis, five to bronchitis, four to abdumi.l discos., four to natural dee., two to hean disease, and one each to cancerous, spinal, anti croup diseases, and one to premature birth. Of the above, eight deaths were children offer years under, and of these seven were thiffiren of one year ihd under. Fifty-one births were registered during the same peribd, making a birth-rate of about 43 per 1000 per arcane. In the corres- ponding month of 1878 there were 43 deaths and 51 birth,.— The report of the medical officer for the last twelvemonths was also read. It was as follows,—oGestlemen,—lt afootes ate pleasure in laying before ran my annual report to be able to congratulate you on rite health of the town of Runcom for the past year, it baying been, to a great extent, Eon from epidemic diseases, and also that the sanitary con- dition han beet, good, and a fair amount of work done to- wards the prevention of febrile dieeas., and.rendering the district more healthy for human habitation ; but yet there is much to be accomplished, and I do hope some time, not tar; hence, to canur the death rate to be much lower than it is at present, via., 22 per 1,1000 ton annum. Taut still of opinion that the atmosphere, impregnated with chemical vapours, , acts as an antiseptic agffinat zymotic diseases, there being I only a few scattered cases daring the year, viz., scarlatilla, 12, meanies, 9, whooping cough, 6; diptheria, 2 ; typhus and typhoid fevers, 1 each. But, on the other hand, 1 believe chemical gas has an injurious effect on persons liable to dis- eases of rly respiraton organs for, on referring to the death returns, I tint there are 80 such cas., viz., 54 attributst Lu bronchitis. 21 to consumption. and five to croup, which, al- though the present year has been an inclement one, I con- alder it an excess to what it ought to Ire. On returning tol another subjec,--infantile mortality—l regret to say that it is enormously high, there being mg of a total of 334 deaths arttnin the rat, IdB which were those of children five pence and mole, elf these 112 were aged one year and under. We all know children are subject t various malaria, but apart from that, I he icon a good deal of the mortality me due to wanton neglect, exposure, the want of suitable clothing, ill-ventilated dwellings, being the off- spring of diee'pated parrots, and, I might sty. also to the huddling together of too many in one room, and the want of cleanlinev In conclusion, I beg to state 'hit, estimating the population approximately 51 14,0 Kt, our death rate Inc the month of November wee ihe lowest of any manufactur- ing town m ,it her England. Ireland, or Scotland, beingonly nine per LOW. I inspected frequemly meat and tish ex- posed for sal., and found nothing wrong. I also inspected and condemned four housm owing to insufficient sanitan accommodation.—Your obedient servant, H. if. Mwralrr.." Mr. NORMAN mid he considered the rep,te very maths Wary. IS A FIRE E.. The Cwatamtw said this was a proposal which, in his opinion, certainly deserved their syrnpathy—(Lear, hoer)— foe they were all day by day, the recipients of the benefits which Sir Rowland Ilill intt.oduced into the postal service of the country. The Highway and Sanitary Committeea contained a report from the Surveyor gating that he had had an interview with the Sehool Board, on the 3rl met., relative to the erection of a boundary wall at the Board School,Heath-road, and had received the following communication from the Clerk : *To Mr. Michael Barker, surveyor, Runcorn. Dec. 9,187 P. Sin—Board School, Heath-roati. I have the honour to state that my Board having carefully considered the subject, as laid before them by you, on the 3rd inst.. are on mimously of opinion that the 156th section of the Public Health Act, 11515. does not apply to this case, inasmuch 10 00 'addition ' to the building is contemplated, but merely the erection of a brick wall to define the boundary. lam to point out to you that the plans, as submitted to yon, have been approved by the Education Department, who, upon the express condition of no alterations in them being made, have recommended the Public Works' Loan Commission,. to advance a suffi- cient sum of money to carry out the proposed im- provement.-1 haw the honour to be, air, your obedient eervant, F.
